newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: Lithuania sees budget balance 2-4 yrs, GDP growth.
newsitem.headline: Lithuania sees budget balance 2-4 yrs, GDP growth.

text.p: Lithuanian Prime Minister Gediminas Vagnorius said his government planned to enshrine a balanced budget amendment in the country's constitution in two to four years.
"We hope to pass a constitutional amendment forbidding a budget deficit in two to four years' time," Vagnorius told Reuters in an interview.
"This year, the budget deficit will be reduced from 3.7 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) to two percent," he said.
"We plan to reduce the deficit steadily every year until we pass the amendment, which will prohibit the deficit," he added.
Vagnorius also expects gross domestic product (GDP) to grow five percent in 1997.
"In 1998, we expect growth of around seven to eight percent," he added.

Lithuania's economy began to grow again in 1994 after a sharp slump sparked by the collapse of the country's trading ties with the former Soviet Union. Preliminary data suggests that GDP grew by four percent in 1996.
Vagnorius expects inflation to be around 12 percent this year and less than 10 percent in 1998 after reaching 13.1 percent in 1996.
The government says it is committed to pursuing prudent fiscal policies and keeping a lid on borrowing.
The budget law currently says that Lithuania's foreign debt, which stood at $1.2 billion at the end of last year, cannot rise by more than $600 million in 1997.
The country plans to issue a $200 million Eurobond later this year, which will be led by JP Morgan Securities.
Vagnorius also said his government was determined to eliminate tax evasion and improve revenue collection.

"We plan to change the tax administration laws and tax procedures...We plan to simplify the tax as much as possible," he said. "We will punish those who conceal their incomes and do not pay taxes...in some circumstances, people will be sentenced to three to five years in prison.
"We must also fight corruption in the law enforcement institutions, such as customs agents and tax inspectors."
Foreign investors working in Lithuania have complained about complicated and excessive taxes and corruption.
A recent survey of foreign businesses operating in Lithuania found dissatisfaction with the legal and tax environment and a widepread perception that bureaucrats were corrupt.
